title: They Returned to the City — the Silver Cup, the Search, the Substitute
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Today I want to put an uncomfortable question to you:
If abandoning somebody were not only possible, but reasonable, and lawful, and nobody at all would blame you for it — what would you do?
In Genesis chapter 44, the silver cup is pulled out of Benjamin's sack. The steward has said it as plainly as it can be said: "He with whom it is found will be my slave; and you will be blameless."

The door stands open. The grain is already loaded on the donkeys. At home there are wives and children waiting. Twenty-two years ago this is exactly how they left: they let one brother go, and they went home with the silver.
But verse 13 of this chapter says, "Then they tore their clothes, and each man loaded his donkey, and returned to the city." They — all eleven of them — went back together.
1. Beginning with the Oldest, Ending at the Youngest

"[Joseph] commanded the steward of his house, saying, 'Fill the men's sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man's money in his sack's mouth. Put my cup, the silver cup, in the sack's mouth of the youngest, with his grain money.'" (Genesis 44:1–2)
And then, "as much as they can carry" — the original reads "according to what they are able to bear." This is not a ration worked out per head. It is a filling right up to the limit.
Grace is given in full first, and only then does the testing begin. That is God's consistent way of working.
And then that silver cup is put into the sack of "the youngest". The text does not give his name — and yet everybody in the room knows exactly who is meant.
They have not gone far when the steward overtakes them: "Why have you rewarded evil for good?"

"Rewarded evil for good" in the original is שִׁלַּמְתֶּם רָעָה תַּחַת טוֹבָה, literally "you have repaid evil in place of good." And that word here for "in place of" — תַּחַת — is the key word of this whole chapter. It is going to come back once more, in verse 33.
The brothers answer in a way that leaves themselves no room at all:

"Why does my lord speak such words as these? Far be it from your servants that they should do such a thing! … Behold, the money, which we found in our sacks' mouths, we brought again to you out of the land of Canaan. How then should we steal silver or gold out of your lord's house? With whomever of your servants it is found, let him die, and we also will be my lord's slaves." (Genesis 44:7–9)
"Far be it" is חָלִילָה in the original, and it is a very heavy word: "May such a thing never be!"

Brothers and sisters, the fuller a man's words, the harder his fall. They put up their own past record as the guarantee — "we brought back every coin the last time" — and then, with their own mouths, they hand down a death sentence.
And the steward takes only half of what they offer: "Now also let it be according to your words. He with whom it is found will be my slave; and you will be blameless."
That sentence is the hinge of the entire test. It hands ten men a perfectly clean way out.
What follows is the most tightly wound passage in the chapter:

"Then they hurried, and each man took his sack down to the ground, and each man opened his sack. He searched, beginning with the oldest, and ending at the youngest. The cup was found in Benjamin's sack." (Genesis 44:11–12)
"Beginning with the oldest" — the original is בַּגָּדוֹל הֵחֵל, "he began with the great one."

Ten sacks, opened one at a time, coming up empty one at a time. Reuben — nothing. Simeon — nothing. Levi — nothing … And every empty sack is one breath of relief and, in the same instant, one more notch of dread.

"Then they tore their clothes." That is the heaviest gesture of grief in the whole Old Testament. In chapter 37 Jacob heard that his son was dead, and tore his clothes; Reuben found the pit empty, and tore his clothes. Once again, this family tears its clothes.
And then those four words: "returned to the city."
Brothers and sisters, in twenty-two years those are the four most important words this family has ever come to.

Twenty-two years ago they left a brother in a pit, sat themselves down to eat their bread, and then went home. Today the opportunity is the same, the reasoning is just as sound, and just as before nobody would have blamed them — and they turn round and go back.
That is the definition of repentance: not merely saying sorry, but making the opposite choice in the same situation.
Why did Joseph set the whole thing up with a silver cup? Doesn't that count as deception?

He had a question that simply had to be asked: if another little son, the one his father loved best, were to fall into trouble, and abandoning him were entirely reasonable, entirely lawful, and nobody would blame them for it — what would they do? A question like that cannot be asked out loud; it can only be set up and laid in front of people. So the steward puts it in the plainest possible words: "He with whom it is found will be my slave; and you will be blameless" — a perfectly clean way out. And notice this: Joseph does not frame anyone in order to have him punished. What he sets in front of them is a choice, and he himself carries the last of the risk — because the moment they walk away, he will never see his brother again.
"As much as they can carry" — what is that little detail doing there?

The original says "according to what they are able to bear" — not a ration worked out per head, but a filling right up to the limit. Grace is given in full first, and only then does the testing begin. That is God's consistent way of working: he does not inspect you first and supply you afterwards; he fills you first and asks his questions afterwards. That helps us in two ways. First, what is already in your hands is usually a great deal more than you think, so when the test comes you do not have to begin by worrying about the grain. Second, anyone who leads can learn this order: before you ask a person to grow, feed him — a person who has not been loved enough cannot stand up under being asked. And for yourself, this verse is also a word of comfort: before the test arrives, God has usually made the provision already.
"Then they tore their clothes … and returned to the city" — why do those four words weigh so much?

Because twenty-two years ago they left a brother in a pit, sat themselves down to eat their bread, and then went home. Today the opportunity is the same, the reasoning is just as sound, and just as before nobody would have blamed them — and yet they turn round and go back, and all eleven of them go back together. That is precisely where the definition of repentance lies: not merely saying sorry, but making the opposite choice in the same situation. So to find out whether a person has really changed, you do not need to listen to how movingly he confesses. You watch which way his feet go the next time he is standing at the same fork in the road. And that is a measure we can lay against ourselves, too.
2. A Light from the Original: God Has Found Out the Iniquity of Your Servants
"Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house, and he was still there. They fell on the ground before him." (Genesis 44:14)
Notice the order of the names in that verse: "Judah and his brothers." This is the first time Judah takes the lead — the first time his name stands out in front.
And this is also the fourth time the dream of chapter 37 comes true.
Joseph puts the question to them, and Judah's answer is the theological summit of the chapter:
"What will we tell my lord? What will we speak? How will we clear ourselves? God has found out the iniquity of your servants." (Genesis 44:16)
"Clear ourselves" is נִצְטַדָּק in the original, and this form of the word occurs only this once in the whole Old Testament — "how can we declare ourselves righteous?"
"Iniquity" is עָוֹן, and this word does not mean "one thing that was done wrong." It means the bent shape of what a person is — that twisted thing on the inside.
And the most important part of it is the subject of the sentence: "God has found out" — הָאֱלֹהִים מָצָא, that God has found it.

Brothers and sisters, this matters enormously. God did not plant that silver cup. Joseph did. And yet what Judah says is not "there is something odd about all this", and it is not "we have been set up."
He knows that on this particular charge they are innocent — but that there is an older account which has never been settled.
He is not confessing the cup. He is confessing the pit, twenty-two years ago.
Sometimes God will use a thing we did not do in order to bring us face to face with a thing we did.
And notice that he says "we" — "the iniquity of your servants" is plural. He does not say, "the cup was in his sack; that is nothing to do with the rest of us."
Then Joseph says, "Far be it from me that I should do so. The man in whose hand the cup is found, he will be my slave; but as for you, go up in peace to your father." (Genesis 44:17)
He uses the very same word they had used: חָלִילָה, "far be it."
And he opens that last door wider still: you may go back "in peace."
This is the final question on the paper: Benjamin stays, the rest of you walk away untouched — and it is the governor of Egypt himself who has said so.
Joseph planted the cup. So why does Judah say, "God has found out the iniquity of your servants"?

Because he knows that on this particular charge they are innocent, and that there is an older account which has never been settled. He is not confessing the cup; he is confessing the pit of twenty-two years ago. And "iniquity" in the original does not mean one thing that was done wrong; it means the bent shape of what a person is — that twisted thing on the inside. Notice, too, that he does not say, "the cup was in his sack; that is nothing to do with the rest of us." What he says is "the iniquity of your servants", in the plural. That gives us a very deep observation: sometimes God will use a thing we did not do in order to bring us face to face with a thing we did. That is not a miscarriage of justice. That is being led.
3. Let Your Servant Stay Instead of the Boy

"Then Judah came near to him, and said, 'Oh, my lord, please let your servant speak a word in my lord's ears, and don't let your anger burn against your servant; for you are even as Pharaoh.'" (Genesis 44:18)
"Came near" is וַיִּגַּשׁ in the original — he took a step forward. Standing in front of a man who is "even as Pharaoh", he did not step back.
What follows is the longest speech in the Old Testament, and the most moving of them all: seventeen verses, delivered in one unbroken breath.
And the strategy of that speech is very much worth our learning.
First, he does not argue the case. From beginning to end he never mentions the silver cup again.

Second, he tells the whole thing over again — starting from "My lord asked his servants, saying, 'Have you a father, or a brother?'" — and step by step he repeats the governor's own words back to him.
Third, he shifts the focus off "Benjamin" and onto "the father".
In this one speech, that way of putting it — "your servant my father" — comes fourteen times.

He says, "his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother; and his father loves him." And "his father loves him", in the original, is precisely the echo of that sentence in chapter 37, verse 4.
Brothers and sisters, hold on to this: Judah is standing there speaking up for the favourite little brother.

Back then it was that very sentence — "his father loves him" — that turned their hearts to murder. Today he takes the same sentence and uses it as his reason, pleading with a stranger to let the boy go.
That wound has healed. This is the clearest evidence there is.
He goes on to say, "your servant my father … his life is bound up in the boy's life."

"Life" is נֶפֶשׁ in the original — not some abstract soul, but the whole living person; and "bound up" is קְשׁוּרָה, literally "tied together." It is the very word 1 Samuel uses when it says that "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David."
"It will happen, when he sees that the boy is no more, that he will die. Your servants will bring down the gray hairs of your servant, our father, with sorrow to Sheol."
"Gray hairs", "Sheol" — both of them are Jacob's own words from chapter 37. Twenty-two years ago they were the ones who caused those words to be spoken; today they are the ones speaking them.
And then comes the summit of the chapter, and the true threshold of this whole story:

"For your servant became collateral for the boy to my father, saying, 'If I don't bring him to you, then I will bear the blame to my father forever.' Now therefore, please let your servant stay instead of the boy, my lord's slave; and let the boy go up with his brothers." (Genesis 44:32–33)
"Instead of the boy" is תַּחַת הַנַּעַר in the original — that same word from verse 4: "in place of."
The man who in chapter 37 said, "Come, and let's sell him to the Ishmaelites", is now saying: make me the slave, and send him home.
The man who once traded a brother for twenty pieces of silver now offers himself in exchange for a brother.
And he adds one more sentence: "For how will I go up to my father, if the boy isn't with me? — lest I see the evil that will come on my father."
He is not doing this so that he can feel better about himself. He simply cannot bear to look at his father's face again.
Brothers and sisters, in the whole of that speech there is not one sentence asking anything for himself. That is what selflessness is.
And this Judah is the ancestor of the Lion. Isaiah 53 says, "Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering … Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all."

Judah was willing to stand in the boy's place, but he never actually did it — Joseph makes himself known in the very next chapter. The one who actually did it is the one who came out of Judah's own tribe: "even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
What is there in the strategy of Judah's speech that is worth learning?

At least three things. First, he does not argue the case — from beginning to end he never mentions the silver cup again, because he knows he cannot win that argument, and that it is not the point anyway. Second, he tells the whole thing over again, repeating the governor's own words back to him step by step, so that the man can see what his own words are about to do. Third, he shifts the focus off "Benjamin" and onto "the father" — in this one speech, "your servant my father" comes fourteen times. That is very mature communication: he does not fight over who is right, he talks about the consequence; he does not talk about himself, he talks about the one who is going to be hurt. And the first thing he does is to "come near" — the original says that he took a step forward. Standing in front of a man who is "even as Pharaoh", he did not step back.
He pleads for the little brother who is "loved by his father". Where does the weight of that lie?

Back then it was that very sentence — "his father loves him" — that turned their hearts to murder; today Judah takes the same sentence and uses it as his reason, pleading with a stranger to let the boy go. That wound has healed — this is the clearest evidence there is. And what he says at the end is, "please let your servant stay instead of the boy, my lord's slave." That word "instead" is exactly the word that stands inside "rewarded evil for good" at the opening of this chapter. The man who once traded a brother for twenty pieces of silver now offers himself in exchange for a brother. In the whole of that speech there is not one sentence asking anything for himself — and that is what selflessness looks like. And he adds one thing more: he cannot bear to look at his father's face again.
I want to go back to that doorway once more.

The most remarkable thing in this chapter is the exit Joseph designed. He does not force them to admit they were wrong. He gives them a chance to leave, and then he watches to see whether they take it.
And this is exactly what God so often does with us.

God will not force you to become good. What he does again and again is to set a perfectly reasonable choice in front of you — a choice for which nobody would blame you — and then wait to see whether you will take it.

That relative you have every right to ignore. That co-worker whose trouble "was his own fault in the first place." That relationship where "I did everything I could anyway." The door is open, and the reasons are more than sufficient.
And what God is waiting for is whether you will turn round and go back.

And let me say the other side of it, so that nobody misunderstands: you are not required to stay every single time. Some relationships are harmful, and leaving is the right thing to do — I said as much when we were in chapter 34. What the text is saying here is not "you may never leave." It is "you may not abandon an innocent person in order to protect yourself."
The way to tell the difference is simple: am I leaving because staying would do harm — or because staying would cost me something?
There is one more thing I want to point out. In verse 16 Judah says, "God has found out the iniquity of your servants" — and in this entire chapter Joseph has not yet told them one word of the truth.
They chose to go back without knowing who this man was, and without knowing whether they would be forgiven.
Real repentance is not something a person does because he already knows he will be pardoned. Real repentance says: even if nothing good comes of it, I am still going to do this right.
Does God use an "open door" to test people? And how am I to tell whether I should stay or go?

The most remarkable thing in this chapter is the exit Joseph designed: he does not force them to admit they were wrong, he gives them a chance to leave and then watches to see whether they take it. God often does the same — he sets in front of you a choice that is perfectly reasonable, and for which nobody would blame you. But let this be said clearly: you are not required to stay every single time. Some relationships are harmful, and leaving is the right thing to do. The way to tell the difference is simple: am I leaving because staying would do harm — or because staying would cost me something? The first is wisdom; the second is self-protection. And where violence or anything unlawful is involved, safety always comes first.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
There are several places in this chapter that need particular care.

The first distortion is to scold Joseph for dishonesty in setting the whole thing up. It was a test, and a necessary one. Its purpose was not entrapment but to see whether they had changed — and before he tested them he had filled their sacks full and put their money back. Blame the method and nothing else, and you have missed the centre of gravity of the whole chapter. The test is this: does the congregation come away seeing scheming, or seeing waiting?

The second distortion is to preach "in place of" as though one human being could atone for another. Judah was willing to stand in the boy's place, but he never actually did it; the one who really stood in our place is the Lion. Blur the two together and the congregation will misunderstand salvation itself. What they should be seeing here is a foreshadowing, and not the substitution itself.

The third distortion is to preach Judah's greatness without preaching his past. This is the man who said, "Come, and let's sell him to the Ishmaelites", and between that sentence and this one lies the confession of chapter 38. Skip over his past and this transformation has no weight at all. The test is this: when the congregation has heard you, do they believe that a person really can change?

The fourth distortion is to preach "they went back to the city together" as though it were the obvious thing to do. Twenty-two years ago these are precisely the men who left a brother behind and walked away. Preach it too lightly and the congregation will not feel that contrast, and so they will not lay hold of what repentance actually means.

The fifth distortion is to preach this chapter as "sacrifice yourself and everything will come out beautifully." When Judah offered to take the boy's place, he did not know how it would end. He was preparing to go and be a slave for the rest of his life. Preach it as a shrewd exchange and you have made sacrifice cheap.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: we are very good at using "that was his own choice" to make letting go sound reasonable. The sibling at home who is forever in some kind of trouble; the co-worker at church who is always dragging the team down — we have a whole set of perfectly sound sentences ready inside us: I have helped him before, he is the one who will not pull himself together, I am under no obligation. Those sentences are not necessarily wrong. But brothers and sisters, what this chapter is asking is not whether your reasoning stands up. It is asking which way you walk when the door opens. This week, write down the name of one person you could reasonably abandon, and then decide: this time I am not abandoning him. Even if it is only one phone call.

The second question: when something goes wrong in our team, our first reaction is to cut ourselves loose. "That was the part he was responsible for." "I did give a warning at the time." Every word of it may be true — but the function of those true words is to get ourselves clean. What Judah said was, "God has found out the iniquity of your servants", and the word he used was "we". Only selflessness can bring unity; and unity is not everybody holding the same opinion, it is everybody willing to carry the thing together. This week, if something goes wrong in your team, say it once: "I have a share in this too."
7. Living 321 Out — Making the Opposite Choice in the Same Situation
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Judah says, "please let your servant stay instead of the boy", and Isaiah says, "Surely he has borne our sickness." The Lord Jesus says, "even as the Son of Man came … to give his life as a ransom for many." My role model is the Lord who stood in my place; and so I am learning to go and stand, just once, in somebody else's place.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "as long as it is reasonable"; the standard is that love "doesn't seek its own way." A great many of the things we do are entirely reasonable and look nothing whatever like love. When what is reasonable collides with what is loving, listen to the standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to stay and when to leave — that takes discernment; it does not come out of one hard rule. Rely on the brain and lean on yourself, and you end up tied in knots, because the brain is better than anything else at manufacturing reasons for self-protection. Rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit, and you end up glad, because the Spirit will let you know who it is you are walking for this time.

Let Jesus be King. "God has found out the iniquity of your servants" — no defending, no deflecting, willing to bear the consequence. To let Jesus be King is to stop dodging the moment the truth is laid out on the table. You do not have to get yourself acquitted, because the one who sits in judgement is at the same time the one who was judged in your place.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. In the whole of Judah's speech there is not one sentence pressing his own case. When a man will not fight for himself, God fights for him: in chapter 49 Jacob says, "The scepter will not depart from Judah", and Revelation says, "the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah … has overcome."

Establish God's system. Eleven men went back to the city together. When you establish God's system it does not show in ordinary weather; it shows the day something goes wrong. The unity of a team is not measured when everyone is celebrating together — it is measured when somebody has to carry the blame.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Open Door
We stand in front of that door carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "I did nothing wrong. Why should I be the one to go back?" And they had done nothing wrong either — they did not put that cup there. And yet what Judah said was, "God has found out the iniquity of your servants." Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, insisting that I will carry a thing only when the fault is mine. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings, willing to carry the thing alongside my brothers even when the fault is not mine.

The fearful heart says, "If I go back, I am finished." And it is true that when they went back, they had no idea how it would turn out. But brothers and sisters, in the moment they turned round, they did not know who was waiting for them inside — it was their own brother, a brother who had already wept over them twice. Behind the door you are most afraid of, very often, grace is standing.

The ashamed heart says, "The thing I did can never be washed off me as long as I live." What Judah did was worse. And in this chapter he is standing right at the front, pleading for his brother. God does not only pardon people; God restores people. He does not merely blot out the sin — he gives you back your place.

The wounded heart says, "I have always been the one who gets left behind." Joseph was the one who was left behind. And in this chapter he stands and listens, sentence by sentence, while his own brother pleads for another brother — until, by the first verse of the next chapter, he cannot hold it in any longer and weeps aloud. If the one who was left behind is willing to wait, there comes a day when he hears that change with his own ears.
Four kinds of heart, one open door. And that door stands open not so that we can escape through it, but so that we can choose.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, towards God. Ask God to give you one chance to "choose again in the same situation", and ask him to let you recognise the moment when it comes.
Second, towards yourself. Write down the name of one person you "could reasonably abandon", and then decide not to abandon him. Do one concrete thing.

Third, towards other people. When something goes wrong in your team, say it once: "I have a share in this too." Do not overstate it, and do not confess on someone else's behalf — simply own the share that is yours.
Fourth, towards daily living. This week, do not use "that was his responsibility" to get yourself clean. Every time that sentence is about to come out of your mouth, stop for three seconds first.
Fifth, towards your mission. Begin praying for one person you never used to care about and now ought to. Once a day, for a full seven days.

Sixth, tell it in three sentences to one friend outside the church. First: there were ten men in the Bible who, twenty-two years ago, dumped their little brother and walked away. Second: twenty-two years later the same opportunity came, and again nobody would have blamed them — and this time they turned round and went back. Third: the reason I believe a person really can change is that I have seen this passage.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer abandon a single person in order to protect myself.
I declare that when something goes wrong, I will say "we", and not "that is his business."
I declare that in the same situation, I will make the opposite choice.
I declare that I am willing to go and stand in somebody else's place, just as my Lord stood in mine.
I am to turn round and go back once this week — but I am afraid it will do no good. What then?

Look at one thing first: when they went back, they still did not know who the man was, and they did not know whether they would be forgiven. They did not go back because they knew how it would end. So "will it do any good" ought not to be the reason that decides it. In practice you can do it like this. First, write down the person you have every right to ignore — that relative, that co-worker, that relationship. Second, do just one concrete thing: one phone call, one visit, one sentence taking your share. Third, once you have done it, hand it over to God, and do not demand that the other person respond straight away. What you get to decide is which way your feet go — not what is standing behind that door.
The door is open. The grain is on the donkeys. The governor of Egypt has said it with his own mouth: "as for you, go up in peace to your father."
They tore their clothes, and returned to the city.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because when Judah said, "please let your servant stay instead of the boy", all he could do was offer; and at Golgotha there was one who actually went and stood there. He did not cry that he had been wronged. He did not argue his case. He did not walk out through the door that stood open for him — "Or do you think that I couldn't ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?" He did not walk. He stayed, and he became the slave in our place.

May God bless every one of us: that in front of that perfectly reasonable door we would choose to turn round and go back; that when something goes wrong in our teams we would be able to say the word "we"; and that all our lives long, again and again, in the same situations, we would make the opposite choice. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson home as a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ Repentance is not merely saying sorry; it is making the opposite choice in the same situation. Which particular thing in your own life does that sentence touch?
2. ★★ God does not force people to become good; he sets a reasonable way out in front of you. What has your door been lately?
3. ★ Grace is given in full first, and only then does the testing begin. What does that order have to say to anyone who leads?
4. ★★ He did not argue the case; he shifted the focus off himself and onto the father. Where could you use that way of speaking?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud ("far be it from your servants that they should do such a thing"), fearful (I am afraid of what it will cost me), ashamed (I walked away once myself), wounded (I am always the one who gets left behind). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "please let your servant stay instead of the boy, my lord's slave." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a door in front of you right now marked "a reasonable way out"? Whether you go or stay — what are you hesitating over?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The person I find it easiest to let go of with a perfectly good reason is …"
9. ★★ This week, for whom will you turn round and go back? Name the one concrete thing you are going to do.

Leader's reminder: do not let this lesson turn into moral pressure. Say it clearly: where a relationship is harmful, leaving is the right thing to do. If someone is currently in a wounding or unsafe relationship, affirm that he is right to keep his distance, and follow up with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own family, who is the one everybody feels free to leave alone? What will you do this week to attend to him, just once?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your ministry, which matter do you most often say "that is not my business" about?

12. ★★★ The practice of standing in someone's place: this week, carry one thing for somebody that he cannot manage himself — and do not let him know that you are the one helping. Say what you are going to do.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him about your door marked "a reasonable way out", and ask him to check with you this week whether you walked through it. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson in three sentences to one friend outside the church. First: there are eleven brothers in the Bible, and the youngest is falsely accused of stealing, and every one of the others could have walked away completely clean. Second: they tore their clothes and turned round and went back together, and one of them said, "let me stay behind as the slave, and send him home." Third: so what I have learned is that the way to tell whether a person has really changed is which way he walks at the same fork in the road. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the door standing open in front of you, and the thing you will turn round and go back to do this week. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to keep us from abandoning anyone in order to protect ourselves, and to give us the wisdom to discern when to stay and when to go.
